  on the earlier half of the test window and
  `r local({ S <- file.path(rprojroot::find_root(rprojroot::has_file("awracing.Rproj")), "_targets_p4"); g <- targets::tar_read(p4_arm_grid_b, store = S)$coefficients; sprintf("%.2f", g$estimate[g$arm == "A1" & grepl("mod", g$term)]) })`

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(targets)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(glue)

# Paper 4 reads the paper-4 store, not the main one. Unlike papers 1-3
# this does NOT call tar_config_set(): that writes the project-root
# `_targets.yaml`, which papers 1-3's own setup chunks also write, and
# pointing it at `_targets_p4` would send their next render at the wrong
# store. Passing `store =` per call leaves `_targets.yaml` untouched.
P4_STORE <- file.path(
  rprojroot::find_root(rprojroot::has_file("awracing.Rproj")),
  "_targets_p4"
)

# tar_load() centrally so tarchetypes::tar_quarto() picks these up as
# render dependencies — files pulled in via {{< include >}} are not
# auto-scanned.
tar_load(c(
  p4_coverage, p4_overround, p4_compression,
  p4_common, p4_floor_report, p4_split_summary,
  p4_arm_grid, p4_arm_grid_b, p4_arm_grid_pooled,
  p4_replication_mod, p4_attenuation,
  p4_amendment2, p4_market_correlations, p4_provenance_facts
), store = P4_STORE)

# ---- accessors -----------------------------------------------------------
# Every number in the prose comes through these, so a mis-typed arm label
# is an error rather than a silently wrong figure.

#' One coefficient row from an arm grid
cf <- function(grid, arm_id, role = c("mod", "mkt")) {
  role <- match.arg(role)
  out <- grid$coefficients |>
    dplyr::filter(arm == arm_id, stringr::str_detect(term, role))
  if (nrow(out) != 1L) {
    stop("cf(): expected 1 row for arm ", arm_id, "/", role,
         ", got ", nrow(out), call. = FALSE)
  }
  out
}

#' One market-only reference fit
mktonly <- function(grid, price_letter) {
  out <- grid$market_only |>
    dplyr::filter(arm == paste0(price_letter, "-mktonly"))
  if (nrow(out) != 1L) stop("mktonly(): bad label", call. = FALSE)
  out
}

#' One likelihood-ratio row
lrow <- function(grid, arm_id) {
  out <- grid$lr |> dplyr::filter(arm == arm_id)
  if (nrow(out) != 1L) stop("lrow(): bad label", call. = FALSE)
  out
}

# Formatters. Deliberately prefixed: short names like `z` or `b` would be
# shadowed by same-named columns inside dplyr verbs.
fmt_b  <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
fmt_ci <- function(row) sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", row$conf_low, row$conf_high)
fmt_z  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
fmt_r2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
comma  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")

n_common  <- length(p4_common$race_ids)
n_test_a  <- p4_split_summary$races[p4_split_summary$half == "A"]
n_test_b  <- p4_split_summary$races[p4_split_summary$half == "B"]
ab_cutoff <- p4_split_summary$cutoff_date[1]

```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Papers 1 to 3 fitted three models to UK All-Weather Flat handicaps — a
conditional logit on Owen's features [@owen2019], the same model on an extended
feature set and a ranking objective, and a gradient-boosted tree ensemble
— and the market outpredicted all three. This paper asks a different
question of the same predictions: not whether the model beats the price,
but whether it adds anything to it.

The construction is a two-stage conditional logit [@benter1994]. A market
probability and a model probability enter a race-conditional logit as
regressors with free coefficients, and the coefficient on the model term,
$\beta_{\text{mod}}$, is the output. If the price already carries
everything the model knows, $\beta_{\text{mod}}$ is zero. If the model
holds information the price does not, it is positive. Papers 1 to 3
cannot measure this: a model that is strictly dominated and a model that
is partly complementary both lose the head-to-head.

The series kept market data out of the feature set so that each change
could be read against the last. Neither price is leakage: the forecast
price is published the evening before a race, and the series has used
starting prices all along to settle its backtests. Here the model still
uses no market data — it is the evaluation that sees the price.

Papers 2a to 3 changed the feature set, the objective and the function
class in turn, and none closed the gap to the market. This paper changes
none of them. It comes before the representation learning paper 3 pointed
toward because it sets that work's bar: if the settled market already
prices what these features carry, a learned representation of the same
run histories has to create information rather than encode it better.

There is no betting-value question here, unlike papers 1 to 3. A blend
that tracks the starting price bets into the starting price's own margin,
so the backtest has a foregone conclusion.

# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

I have been interested in modelling horse racing since first
acquiring the Smartform database more than a decade ago. The project
has been picked up and put down many times, the obstacle almost
always being the gap between an idea and a running implementation.
What is different now is that working alongside Claude Code
(Anthropic's coding agent), with web-based Claude as a research
companion, has compressed that gap dramatically. I am grateful to
my brother, Michael Gillen, for the suggestion to build the model
on All-Weather races — the foundation of the scope choices set out
in paper 1. The design choices — dataset, scope, model, comparison,
editorial line — are mine. The implementation, the bulk of the draft
prose, and a great deal of the verification were Claude Code's, under
my direction; every output was reviewed and edited before it reached
the paper. I do not yet know what general lessons this experiment
points to about the value of human–AI collaboration in applied
statistics. That uncertainty is part of why I am doing the work, and
these papers are partly a record of that experiment.
